item.title: Emotion regulation abilities among people who use electronic cigarettes, tobacco cigarettes, or both
item.description:
Background: Emotion regulation difficulties can hinder nicotine cessation. Although people who smoke tobacco cigarettes struggle to regulate negative emotions using cognitive reappraisal, whether people who use electronic cigarettes experience similar difficulties remains unknown. We therefore compared the cognitive reappraisal abilities of people who use electronic cigarettes on a daily basis, with the abilities of people who use tobacco cigarettes daily, people who use both products daily, and people who use neither.

Methods: Between March and September 2025, 53 people who use electronic cigarettes daily, 50 people who use tobacco cigarettes daily, 52 people who use both nicotine products daily and 50 people who use neither were all recruited through Prolific Academic and completed an online cognitive reappraisal task and the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), administered via Gorilla. Group differences in reappraisal success and DERS scores were examined using ANOVAs, while relationships with nicotine use behaviours were assessed using partial correlations. All analyses controlled for age, gender, alcohol use and cannabis use.

Results: People who use neither electronic or tobacco cigarettes exhibited greater reappraisal success than all three nicotine-using groups, which did not differ from one another. Further, greater self-reported electronic cigarette consumption was associated with poorer reappraisal success, whereas no such relationship was observed for daily tobacco cigarette use. Finally, there were no group effects on, or relationships between nicotine use and, DERS scores.

Conclusions: This study provides the first evidence that people who use electronic cigarettes show cognitive reappraisal difficulties comparable to those who use tobacco cigarettes. These findings may have implications for developing psychological interventions to support electronic cigarette cessation, although further research is required to establish their relevance to quitting outcomes.

item.title: Energy landscape analysis reveals constrained attractor dynamics linked to alcohol-use severity in alcohol use disorder
item.description:
Background: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) involves large-scale brain network dysregulation. However, conventional connectivity approaches provide limited insight into how the brain enters, maintains, and switches between functional states. We applied energy landscape analysis to characterize attractor-like dynamics in AUD.

Methods: We analyzed resting-state fMRI data from 93 individuals with AUD and 91 matched healthy control participants from the Human Connectome Project. Regional time series were summarized into eight functional systems and modeled using a pairwise maximum entropy model. We identified attractor-like states and quantified occupancy and transition rates. Group comparisons used false discovery rate correction; clinical relevance was assessed using partial correlation, moderation, and mediation analyses.

Results: The model identified six attractor-like states, including two primary states interpreted as putative sensory-attentional (B1) and affective-reward-related (B6) configurations based on their network profiles. AUD was associated with reduced bidirectional transitions between B1 and B6, reduced occupancy of B1 and B6, and greater occupancy of an intermediate state, B4. Exploratory AUD-only analyses showed nominal associations of lower B6 occupancy with more frequent heavy drinking and of reduced B1 occupancy and fewer B1-to-B6 transitions with greater recent weekend alcohol consumption. AUD status moderated the B1-to-B6 transition-weekend alcohol consumption relationship, and B1 occupancy partially accounted for associations between AUD status and recent drinking and alcohol dependence status.

Conclusions: Energy landscape analysis revealed constrained attractor dynamics in AUD, with reduced transition rates between putative sensory-attentional and affective-reward-related configurations and redistribution toward an intermediate state. These findings highlight the clinical relevance of altered state dynamics in AUD.

item.title: Comparing the single-item screen-cannabis (SIS-C) with brief cannabis screening questions for identifying cannabis use disorder
item.description:
Objectives: Compare performance of a validated Single-Item Screen-Cannabis (SIS-C) for cannabis use disorder (CUD) completed in primary care (PC) versus competed for research, and to compare the SIS-C (assessing past-year frequency of use) to alternative brief cannabis screens.

Methods: Adult PC patients who completed the SIS-C (3/28/2019-9/12/2019) in a Washington health system, were randomly sampled for a confidential survey. Participant responses (n = 1688) were linked to electronic health records (EHRs). CIDI-SAM, completed via survey, was the reference standard for any CUD and moderate-severe CUD. Screens included: (1) SIS-C completed in routine PC and documented in EHRs ("clinical SIS-C"); (2) SIS-C completed via survey not shared with providers ("research SIS-C"); (3) question assessing typical times-per-day of use completed via survey; and (4) composite measure combining frequency and times-per-day. Weighted analyses estimated sensitivity, specificity, and AUC of screens compared to CUD on the CIDI-SAM, estimating differences between AUCs (∆AUC) with confidence limits.

Results: Past-year CUD prevalence was 6.6% (1.9% moderate-severe). All screens demonstrated excellent discrimination for any and moderate-severe CUD (AUC≥ 0.80). Performance of the clinical SIS-C and research SIS-C did not differ for any CUD (ΔAUC -0.025 [95% CI -0.119-0.046]) while the clinical SIS-C performed slightly better for moderate-severe CUD (ΔAUC 0.024 [0.009-0.043]). The research SIS-C outperformed the times-per-day item, and the composite measure offered minimal improvement over frequency alone.

Conclusions: The SIS-C performed similarly in routine PC and research contexts. Adding a times-per-day question did not meaningfully improve performance. Findings support SIS-C use to identify patients at risk of CUD.

item.title: The association of state cannabis legalization with polysubstance use disorders involving cannabis use disorder
item.description:
Objectives: To examine associations of state medical and recreational cannabis legalization (MCL, RCL) with polysubstance use disorders involving cannabis use disorder (CUD).

Methods: Using quasi-experimental difference-in-differences models with staggered adoption, we analyzed 2010-2022 Merative MarketScan Commercial Claims data for adults aged 18-64. Outcomes included: (1) prevalence of co-occurring CUD and alcohol, opioid, or tobacco use disorders (AUD, OUD, TUD) within the same quarter; (2) incident CUD diagnoses among patients with past-year AUD, OUD, or TUD; and (3) incident AUD, OUD, or TUD diagnoses among patients with past-year CUD. Incident cases were defined using a 6-month look-back period.

Findings: No significant associations were observed between cannabis legalization and prevalence of co-occurring CUD and AUD or TUD. Compared to states without cannabis legalization, RCL was associated with a 66.93% (coefficient=-8.26; 95%CI: -15.90,-0.62; P < 0.05) reduction in prevalence of co-occurring CUD and OUD. Among patients with past-year CUD, MCL and RCL were associated with 14.43% (coefficient=-0.14; 95%CI: -0.27,-0.010; P < 0.05) and 22.68% (coefficient=-0.22; 95%CI: -0.39,-0.045; P < 0.05) reductions in incident AUD diagnoses, and 20.73% (coefficient=-0.13; 95%CI: -0.25,-0.013; P < 0.05), and 44.61% (coefficient=-0.29; 95%CI: -0.48,-0.10; P < 0.01) reductions in incident OUD diagnoses, respectively. RCL was associated with a 34.44% (coefficient=0.062; 95%CI: 0.20,0.10; P < 0.01) increase in incident CUD diagnoses among patients with past-year TUD.

Conclusions: Polysubstance use disorder patterns shifted in the U.S. following state cannabis legalization. During 2010-2022, MCL and RCL were associated with lower incidence of AUD and OUD among patients with past-year CUD, while RCL was associated with higher incidence of CUD among patients with past-year TUD.

item.title: A community-led compassion club as an alternative to illicit drug markets: Pricing and changes in high-intensity drug use
item.description:
Objectives: In 2022, the Drug User Liberation Front (DULF) began operating a non-medicalized safer supply compassion club (CC) where members could purchase rigorously tested illicit cocaine, heroin and methamphetamine at cost. The present study sought to compare DULF CC drug prices with local street prices and examine the association between enrollment in the DULF CC and high-intensity drug use.

Methods: An economic analysis compared the prices of DULF CC drugs with prevailing street-market prices reported by participants in the Vancouver Injection Drug Users Study (VIDUS), a community-recruited prospective cohort of people who use drugs in Vancouver. Generalized estimating equation (GEE) logistic regression analyses were used to examine the association between CC enrollment and self-reported high-intensity (≥daily vs. <daily) use of methamphetamine, cocaine and opioids, respectively, among a prospective cohort of DULF CC participants.

Results: During the August 2022 to October 2023 study period, DULF CC drugs were found to be consistently less expensive and less variable in price than their street-market counterparts. In multivariable GEE analyses, enrollment in the DULF CC was associated with significantly lower odds of high-intensity methamphetamine use (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 0.49, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.29-0.82; p = 0.007) and high-intensity opioid use (AOR = 0.56, 95% CI: 0.37-0.85; p = 0.006), while no significant association was observed for high-intensity cocaine use.

Discussion: Findings suggest that the DULF CC provided community-regulated drugs at lower and more stable prices than those available through illicit markets, and that enrollment was associated with reductions in opioid and methamphetamine use.

Nyx E, Kalicum J, Hayashi K, Mok WY, Kerr T, Kennedy MC

item.title: Social control of cocaine intake: Sex differences in behavioral vs. cocaine-exposure cues
item.description:
Background: Drug taking is influenced by social partners, but the social cues that control another individual's drug use remain unclear.

Objective: The present study determined whether cocaine self-administration is influenced more by a partner's level of cocaine-maintained responding or by the partner's level of cocaine intake.

Methods: Male and female rats were assigned to same-sex observer-model dyads. Following initial cocaine self-administration training, observer rats self-administered 0.3mg/kg/infusion cocaine under a fixed-ratio 1 schedule throughout testing. One group of models self-administered cocaine under individualized variable-ratio (VR) schedules that maintained high rates of lever pressing, with each model tested at 0.1, 0.3, and 1.0mg/kg/infusion. A second group received cocaine noncontingently (NT) and was yoked to the VR models, receiving the same number and timing of cocaine infusions without lever pressing.

Results: Observer responding varied as a function of model schedule, cocaine dose, and sex. In male observer rats, responding followed an inverted-U-shaped function across model dose in the VR condition, closely paralleling partner lever pressing, but remained unchanged across dose in the NT condition. In contrast, female observer responding increased with model cocaine dose under both VR and NT conditions, paralleling partner cocaine intake.

Conclusions: These findings indicate that features of a cocaine-using social partner can differentially influence cocaine self-administration in male and female rats. Under these conditions, the responding of male observers was more strongly controlled by the partner's level of cocaine-maintained responding, whereas the responding of female observers was more closely related to the partner's level of cocaine intake.

item.title: The role of early school performance on subsequent alcohol and drug use disorders: A Swedish cohort study
item.description:
Aims: To examine whether lower academic performance in compulsory school (age 15-16) increases the risk of later alcohol use disorder (AUD) and drug use disorder (DUD), and to assess the extent to which shared familial factors account for these associations.

Methods: This national cohort study included 2937,919 individuals born in Sweden between 1972 and 2002, residing in Sweden on 1 July of the year in which school grades were assessed (ages 15-16 years), followed until first diagnosis of AUD without comorbid DUD, DUD without comorbid AUD, death, or December 31, 2023. Academic performance was measured using 9th-grade grade point average and categorized into deciles. Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs), and sibling-comparison models were used to adjust for shared familial genetic and environmental factors FINDINGS: Lower academic performance was strongly associated with increased risk of both AUD and DUD, showing a clear dose-response pattern across the full grade distribution. Risks were consistently higher for DUD than for AUD, and the associations remained robust in sibling-comparison analyses, although somewhat attenuated.

Conclusion: Lower academic performance in adolescence is a strong predictor of later AUD and DUD, with markedly higher risks for DUD. Neither birth year, sex, maternal and paternal psychiatric history, parental income, nor the highest parental education origin, nor shared familial factors fully explain the association.

item.title: Comparative effectiveness and safety of generic versus brand-name varenicline for smoking cessation in Chinese population: Findings from China National Tobacco Cessation Cohort Study (CNTCCS)
item.description:
Background: Following the global withdrawal of brand-name varenicline due to nitrosamine contamination, generic formulations have become the only available varenicline option for smoking cessation in China. To compare the real-world effectiveness and safety of generic versus brand-name varenicline for smoking cessation in China.

Methods: We conducted a nationwide, multicenter, historical-comparator cohort analysis using data from the China National Tobacco Cessation Cohort Study (CNTCCS). The primary outcome was biochemically validated 7-day point prevalence abstinence at 24 weeks. Secondary outcomes included continuous abstinence, medication adherence, and adverse reactions. A modified Intention-to-treat analyses were performed.

Results: Among 1209 participants, 256 initiated generic varenicline and 953 initiated brand-name varenicline; 512 participants were included after matching. At 24 weeks, validated abstinence rates were similar between generic and brand-name varenicline both before matching (33.2% vs. 33.8%) and after matching (33.2% vs. 33.2%). Medication adherence declined over time in both groups and was comparable throughout follow-up (all P > 0.05). However, adverse reactions were more frequently reported with generic varenicline (32.4% vs. 12.1% at week 1; 18.0% vs. 7.0% at week 12; all P < 0.001), although no serious adverse events occurred in either group.

Conclusions: In this historical-comparator cohort analysis, generic and brand-name varenicline demonstrated similar smoking cessation effectiveness at 24 weeks. Generic varenicline was associated with a higher frequency of nonserious adverse reactions, highlighting the importance of monitoring tolerability in routine clinical practice. These findings support the continued use of generic varenicline for smoking cessation following the withdrawal of the brand-name product.

Liu Z, Ji TF, Cheng AQ, Wang M, Song QQ, Zhou XM
